Absolute-value placement in the printed intermediate proof is recoverable by the displayed magnitude bound.

checks.claim: \kappa\geq\frac{\sum_{k\in[K]}\eta^{(k)}/\kappa^{(k)}}{\sum_{k\in[K]}\eta^{(k)}}
checks.explanation: The written average of reciprocals is at most one. Therefore every \(\kappa\geq1\) satisfies the displayed condition, whatever the actual occupancy mismatch. Telescoping gives \((\min_kG^{(k)})\sum_k\eta^{(k)}/\kappa^{(k)}\leq B\). To derive \(\min_kG^{(k)}\leq\kappa B/\sum_k\eta^{(k)}\), one needs \(\sum_k\eta^{(k)}/\kappa^{(k)}\geq\sum_k\eta^{(k)}/\kappa\), which is equivalent to the required harmonic-mean bound \(\kappa\geq(\sum_k\eta^{(k)})/(\sum_k\eta^{(k)}/\kappa^{(k)})\). The written condition has numerator and denominator interchanged and cannot justify the last division in Lemma 10. This is a proof/assumption failure, not a demonstrated lower bound on the algorithm complexity.
checks.demonstration: If all \(\kappa^{(k)}=9\), the stated condition permits \(\kappa=1\); the needed harmonic coefficient is nine. Valid occupancy laws such as \((.9,.1)\) against \((.1,.9)\) attain that maximum ratio.
checks.repair: Invert the displayed ratio in Assumption 4 and carry that precise condition through the Lemma 10 division and theorem complexity statement. Verify finiteness on zero-occupancy states using an explicit ratio convention.
checks.scope: The written concentrability assumption does not justify the final telescoping bound. The corrected assumption supplies the required denominator comparison.
checks.whyItMatters: The written condition is automatic for any coefficient at least one and does not justify the claimed dependence on that coefficient.
checks.title: The concentrability condition bounds the wrong reciprocal average
checks.claimContext: Assumption 4 bounds a weighted mean of reciprocal occupancy-mismatch coefficients. Lemma 10 later uses that condition to remove those coefficients from its telescoping denominator.

checks.claim: \mathbf{1}\left\{a_{i}\in\arg\max_{a_{i}^{\prime}}\hat{Q}^{(k)}_{i,h}(w_{i},a_{i}^{\prime})\right\}
checks.explanation: Let \(A^*(w)=\arg\max_a\widehat Q(w,a)\). Summing the displayed update gives \(1-\eta+\eta|A^*(w)|\), so any tie with \(\eta>0\) produces mass greater than one. Take a one-player, one-state, one-observation finite-horizon POMG with two actions and identically zero rewards. The potential is zero, every belief is the same (hence filter contraction holds), the observation lower bound holds with \(\beta=1\), and all policies are best responses. At horizon one the superstate occupancy is one independently of the policy, so the concentrability condition holds with coefficient one. Every empirical reward and backward Q value is exactly zero, including the stipulated zero values for unobserved pairs. The theorem assumptions impose no unique-maximizer condition or single-action tie rule. Thus this permitted game gives two maximizing actions and the written update leaves the policy simplex at its first positive step. This is a failure to define the theorem-named policy update, not a claim that an appropriately normalized greedy update cannot learn an equilibrium.
checks.demonstration: For \(\pi=(1/2,1/2)\), \(\eta=1/5\), and tied Q values, line 10 gives \((3/5,3/5)\), whose total mass is \(6/5\).
checks.repair: Select one maximizer \(a^*(w)\) by a fixed tie rule and use \(\mathbf1\{a=a^*(w)\}\), or replace the indicator by any probability distribution supported on the maximizing-action set. Either choice stays in the simplex and retains the greedy expected-Q value. A unique-maximizer assumption also suffices but excludes valid tied games unnecessarily.
checks.scope: The theorem-named update fails probability-simplex validity on an admissible tie. A normalized greedy update repairs this local defect.
checks.whyItMatters: On an allowed tie, the displayed update assigns total probability greater than one and therefore does not define the next policy.
checks.title: The policy update is not normalized when more than one action maximizes Q
checks.claimContext: Theorem 1 names Algorithm 1 as its policy update. Line 10 adds the membership indicator of the entire maximizing-action set, so tied actions must be checked against the probability-simplex requirement.

checks.claim: \left\lVert b_{h}(\cdot\mid\tau)-b_{h^{\prime}}(\cdot\mid\tau^{\prime})\right\rVert_{TV}\leq(1-\rho)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}m-1}}
checks.explanation: Take one player, two states, one action, one uninformative observation, zero rewards, horizon at least three. Let the stage-one transition reset to state zero and stage-two transition reset to state one, independently of the incoming state. Each within-stage belief-update map is constant, so it satisfies Assumption 2 for \(\rho=1/2\) (indeed for any \(\rho\leq1\)). All symbolic histories are identical. For \(m=2,h=2,h^{\prime}=3\), the beliefs are \(\delta_0,\delta_1\) and their TV distance is one, greater than \(1/2\). Applying the contraction at different stages is invalid because the maps differ. For \(h=h^{\prime}\), the usual \(m-1\) common updates do give the stated bound.
checks.demonstration: The reset-kernel construction meets decoupledness and the potential assumption (zero rewards); singleton observations are uninformative rather than state revealing. The failure is the cross-time quantifier, not the exponent \(m-1\).
checks.repair: Restrict Lemma 3 to \(h=h^{\prime}\), with both histories reachable at that common stage, and verify that each intended application has this time alignment. A cross-time version requires a common filtering map with a contraction guarantee for every relevant pair of priors, including any restarted-window priors. Time homogeneity alone does not establish that stronger all-priors guarantee.
checks.scope: Lemma 3 needs a time-aligned statement or stronger filter assumptions. This counterexample alone does not refute the main learning theorem.
checks.whyItMatters: Same symbolic observations at different stages need not correspond to the same filtering maps.
checks.title: Same-window filter contraction is not a cross-time guarantee for nonstationary kernels
checks.claimContext: Lemma 3 applies the same-window belief bound to histories ending at potentially different absolute times, although the model allows time-dependent transition and observation kernels.

checks.location: Appendix E.1, Algorithm 3 finite Armijo limit
checks.claim: The finite-J line search guarantees sufficient ascent for each accepted update.
checks.explanation: Smoothness guarantees eventual acceptance only when sufficiently small steps remain available. A fixed trial cap does not supply that guarantee.
checks.demonstration: Let the underlying loss be zero and the penalized objective \(h(z)=-\lambda z^2\), anchored at zero. Start at \(z=1\); the initial BB secant vanishes, so the initial fallback step is used. The gradient is \(-2\lambda\), and an ascent step is \(z^+=1-2\lambda\eta\). If the finite halving schedule still has \(\lambda\eta>1\), then \(|z^+|>1\) and \(h(z^+)<h(1)\). The existing witness uses \(\lambda=10^8\) and the printed defaults; every permitted trial fails before the unconditional update.

checks.location: Definition 2.3, zero Monge gap iff support-wise cyclical monotonicity
checks.claim: Zero gap for arbitrary Borel T is equivalent to cyclical monotonicity at every support point.

checks.contextBefore: Robustness to image corruptions. We evaluate on CIFAR-10-C [35], which features $15$ algorithmic corruptions (e.g., noise, blur, weather effects) at five severity levels. As shown in Table 1, ICNN-DRO attains $82.77\%$ average accuracy, outperforming PA ( $79.20\%$ ) and WFR ( $81.10\%$ ). Notably, it exceeds ERM ( $81.92\%$ ), showing that robustification via a global transport map improves resilience to corruptions without sacrificing in-distribution accuracy. The gap widens at the highest severity (level $5$ ), where ICNN-DRO reaches $73.95\%$ against $69.74\%$ for PA.
